title: What the Church Got Wrong About Race, and What Scripture Said All Along
excerpt: American pulpits defended slavery and then segregation with open Bibles, while Black Christians read the same book and heard the God of the Exodus. The texts had been plain the whole time.
body:
A Black Christian walks into a church where every other face is white and wonders how long the welcome will last. A white Christian hears the word racism from the pulpit and stiffens, sure he is about to be blamed for things done before he was born. And a skeptic who knows some history watches them both and asks a fair question: why should anyone take moral instruction from an institution that needed a war to learn that people cannot be owned?

Each of them is reacting to something real. The first is remembering what churches have done. The second is right that guilt cannot simply be handed down like a surname, though that is not the whole of what Scripture says about the sins of fathers. The skeptic has the history mostly right. The church in America did not merely fail to stop racial slavery and the segregation that followed it. A large part of the church defended both, by name, from the Bible. Anyone who wants to say what Scripture teaches about race has to begin by admitting who taught the opposite.

## The Pulpits That Defended It

The trouble started early. English colonists in the 1600s were uneasy about holding fellow Christians as slaves, and that unease could have become a conscience. In 1667 the Virginia assembly settled the matter the other way, with a law declaring that baptism did not change whether a person was slave or free. A man could now be a brother at the font and property at the auction. The line between who could be owned and who could not had to be drawn somewhere else, and it was drawn at color.

By the 1840s the question was splitting denominations. In 1844 the Methodist General Conference learned that one of its bishops, James O. Andrew of Georgia, had come to own slaves, and it asked him to stop exercising his office while he did. The Southern conferences refused the rebuke and organized the Methodist Episcopal Church, South, the next year. Baptists divided at almost the same moment. When the mission board in Boston made it clear that it would not appoint a slaveholder as a missionary, Baptists from the slaveholding states met in Augusta, Georgia, in May 1845 and founded a convention of their own. These were among the largest Protestant bodies in the country. They broke apart sixteen years before the nation did, and over the same thing.

The men who led the Southern side were not embarrassed. They believed the Bible was with them, and they said so in print. In 1860 a publisher in Augusta issued a thick volume of proslavery writing that included an essay by Thornton Stringfellow, a Baptist minister in Virginia. Stringfellow began with Noah. After the flood, Noah's son Ham dishonored his father, and Noah answered with a curse and two blessings. From that passage Stringfellow concluded that "God decreed slavery," and that the decree showed "tokens of good-will to the master." He identified the cursed line as "the Canaanites or Africans, who descended from Ham." Then he went on through Abraham's household, the law of Moses, and Paul's instructions to servants, which gave him the stronger part of his case.

That reading of Genesis is usually called the curse of Ham, and it did a great deal of work. It took a system built on kidnapping and profit and made it look like the outworking of prophecy. It told the slaveholder that the color line was older than Virginia and that God himself had drawn it.

## What Genesis Actually Says

The passage is short enough to check. Noah wakes, learns what Ham has done, and says, "Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be to his brothers" (Genesis 9:25).

The curse falls on Canaan, who is one of Ham's four sons. It does not fall on Ham, and it does not fall on Ham's other sons, whom the next chapter names as Cush, Egypt and Put (Genesis 10:6), the peoples of Africa as Israel knew them. The Canaanites lived in the land of Canaan, on the eastern shore of the Mediterranean. The speaker is Noah, a man just waking from drunkenness, and the text never says God stood behind his words. Nothing in the chapter mentions skin. Nothing in it mentions Africa. For Israel's first hearers the point of the story was near at hand, because it concerned the peoples they were about to meet in the land.

To get from Genesis 9 to a cotton field, a reader has to move the curse from the son to the father, spread it from one grandson to a continent, and stretch it across four thousand years. Stringfellow's phrase "Canaanites or Africans" does all of that with one small word. He was not a careless reader. He read every other passage in his essay with close attention. He misread this one because his whole society needed him to.

## After Slavery, the Same Habit

The war ended slavery, and it didn't end the reading. For another century white churches across the South, and many in the North, accepted the color line as the natural order and often called it God's. The curse of Ham was preached again, now in defense of separation. Congregations that sent missionaries to Africa seated Black visitors in the balcony or turned them away at the door.

That habit was old too. Richard Allen was born into slavery in 1760 and was converted under Methodist preaching. He bought his freedom and became a preacher in Philadelphia. By his own account, around 1787 he and Absalom Jones and other Black members were kneeling in prayer in the gallery of their Methodist church when white trustees pulled them up from their knees and told them they were in the wrong seats. They walked out together. Allen's congregation, Bethel, was dedicated in 1794, and in 1816 Black Methodist congregations from several cities organized the African Methodist Episcopal Church with Allen as its first bishop.

White Christians sometimes speak of the historically Black churches as though they were a regrettable division in the body of Christ. They are a division. They exist because men were dragged off their knees for praying in the wrong pew.

In April 1963 Martin Luther King Jr., a Baptist preacher, sat in a jail cell in Birmingham, Alabama, and wrote a long letter to white clergymen of that city who had publicly urged him to wait. The letter is easy to find and should be read whole. Its sharpest disappointment is not with the open defenders of segregation. It is with moderate white Christians who agreed that segregation was wrong, preferred order to justice, and kept telling their Black brothers that the time was not yet right. He was describing a great many white churches. In 1995 the denomination founded in Augusta said so itself, in a resolution confessing that its beginning was bound up with the defense of slavery and that it had defended segregation in the generations after.

## What Scripture Said All Along

None of this was hidden in a hard passage. The Bible's teaching about human beings begins on its first page: "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them" (Genesis 1:27). The verse is spoken over the one pair from whom everyone comes. It has no second sentence for lesser peoples.

Paul said the same thing in Athens, a city proud of the old story that its people had sprung from its own soil and were a breed apart: "And he made from one man every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth" (Acts 17:26). Scripture speaks of nations, tribes, peoples and languages. It has no category that sorts human beings into higher and lower kinds by color. That idea, race as most of us learned it, grew up in the same centuries as the Atlantic slave trade and served it.

The New Testament's first great fight was over this very thing in another form. When Peter stopped eating with Gentile believers at Antioch because of pressure from his own group, Paul "opposed him to his face" (Galatians 2:11) and said that such conduct "was not in step with the truth of the gospel" (Galatians 2:14). He did not treat a separate table as a regrettable custom. He treated it as a denial of what Christ had done. In the same letter he wrote, "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28). He told the Ephesians that Christ "is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility" (Ephesians 2:14).

And the Bible ends where it was always going. John sees "a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb" (Revelation 7:9). The differences are still visible in that crowd, which means they were never the problem. The ranking was the problem.

Some heard it. In 1794 Allen and Jones published an address to slaveholders, and one sentence in it answers Stringfellow sixty-six years before he was reprinted: "We wish you to consider, that God himself was the first pleader of the cause of slaves." In the same pamphlet they thanked those white Christians who were not ashamed to call Black men and women "children of one father, who made of one blood all the nations of the earth." That is Acts 17:26, nearly as their King James Bible gave it. In 1845 Frederick Douglass, seven years out of slavery, drew the line that still has to be drawn: "between the Christianity of this land, and the Christianity of Christ, I recognize the widest possible difference."

Enslaved people were taught the Bible so that they would obey. They heard in it the God who brought Israel out of Egypt. They kept the faith of the men who whipped them and kept it more truly, and that is one of the strangest and strongest facts in the history of the church.

## How Sincere People Missed It

It would be a comfort to think the defenders of slavery and segregation were hypocrites who knew better. Most of them were not. They prayed, they gave, they loved their children, and they could not see it. Their wealth depended on not seeing it, and so did their place in the community and their peace of mind. Their preachers were paid by the people who needed the comfortable reading. The Bible was read in rooms where no Black Christian was allowed to answer back.

Jesus described this exactly. He spoke of people who decorate the tombs of the prophets and say, "If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have taken part with them in shedding the blood of the prophets" (Matthew 23:30). Every reader of this history is tempted to say the same sentence. We would have stood with Allen. We would have marched in Birmingham. The honest guess is that most of us would have done what most Christians of our kind did, and would have had a verse ready. The useful question is which of our own readings are being held in place right now by what they protect.

## What Repair Requires

Here Christians who agree on everything above part ways, and the disagreement should be described without contempt for either side.

Some hold that the remedy for racism is the gospel doing what it has always done. Sin lives in the heart, the new birth changes hearts, and the place where the dividing wall comes down is the local church, at a shared table, over years. They point out that Scripture refuses inherited guilt: "The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father" (Ezekiel 18:20). They fear that sorting people into guilty and innocent groups by color repeats the old error with the labels reversed, and that a church which takes its categories from the politics of the hour has stopped preaching Christ.

Others hold that repentance in Scripture is rarely that private. Daniel had not built the high places, and he prayed, "To us, O Lord, belongs open shame, to our kings, to our princes, and to our fathers, because we have sinned against you" (Daniel 9:8). Nehemiah confessed that "I and my father's house have sinned" (Nehemiah 1:6). Zacchaeus did not only feel sorry. He said, "if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold" (Luke 19:8), and Jesus answered, "Today salvation has come to this house" (Luke 19:9). On this view, wrongs that were written into deeds, loans, schools and church budgets left damage that outlived the people who did them, and a church that inherited the buildings also inherited some of the bill. They fear that talk of changed hearts, with nothing changed outside the heart, is the moderate's old counsel of patience in new words.

Each side sees something the other is in danger of losing. The first is right that no program can do what the Spirit does, and that the church must not trade one ranking of human beings for another. The second is right that the Bible knows corporate sin, and that sorrow which costs nothing is not what Scripture means by repentance. There is a further disagreement among Black Christians themselves, between those who long to see congregations where every people worships together and those who will not give up churches that were, for two centuries, the one institution their people owned. That one deserves to be heard and not managed.

## What Is Settled and What Is Not

Some of this is not open. Every human being bears the image of God. The human race is one family. To rank people by ancestry or color is what James calls partiality: "if you show partiality, you are committing sin" (James 2:9). The church is one body drawn from every nation, and Paul counted a segregated table a contradiction of the gospel itself. These things are tied to what the creeds confess about creation and about the one church. The curse of Ham as a warrant for slavery or separation was a false teaching, and it should be called that.

What repair requires in a given town, a given congregation, or a given budget is a different kind of question. Faithful Christians weigh it differently, and they can do so without calling each other racists or heretics. What they can't do is use the disagreement as a reason to do nothing.

The skeptic at the beginning of this essay asked why he should listen to an institution with this record. He is owed a plain answer. The record is ours. The book we misused was against us the whole time, and the people we wronged were the ones who read it rightly. At the end of that book there is a crowd no one can number, from every tribe and people and language. The people our churches turned away at the door are standing in it. The question that remains is whether we will have learned to stand beside them before we get there.

*"So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them."* (Genesis 1:27)

*"For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility."* (Ephesians 2:14)
